places.address: West side of Church St between Cherry and Bank (block overview)

timeline.what: Three structures on Young's village plan
timeline.detail: Ammi B. Young's 1830 Plan of Burlington Village showed only three structures on the five plots on this side of the block.
timeline.quote: Of the five plots outlined along the west side of Church Street there were only three structures built.

timeline.detail: John Johnson's 1833 survey showed the same layout as Young's 1830 plan.
timeline.quote: A survey conducted by Johnson in 1833 showed the same plan three years following Young’s Plan of Burlington Village.

timeline.detail: By the 1869 Sanborn map almost all residential structures had been demolished for the Central Block, Union Block, and Central House.
timeline.quote: In 1869 when the Sanborn Fire Insurance Map (Figure 1) was released almost all evidence of residential structures along the west side of Church Street between Cherry and Bank Streets had been demolished

timeline.detail: Many shopfronts received glass canopies in 1981, with brickwork laid in the early 1980s.
timeline.quote: Like many shopfronts on Church Street, a glass canopy was added in 1981 to the front of the building

photos.caption: 1869 Sanborn fire insurance map showing the area of study

timeline.detail: A two and a half story brick dwelling stood on the northwest corner of Cherry and Church; its footprint appears on the 1853 Presdee & Edwards map.
timeline.quote: Visual evidence of the building’s footprint is seen in the 1853 Presdee & Edwards Map of Burlington on the northwest corner of Cherry and Church Streets.

timeline.what: Griswold home, then J. A. Shedd
timeline.detail: The brick dwelling was William A. Griswold's home and later J. A. Shedd's firm and residence; no years given.
timeline.quote: This brick dwelling was the home of William A. Griswold and later the firm and residence of J. A. Shedd.

timeline.detail: The 1885 Sanborn map confirms the corner residence was brick; the page says residences survived on these blocks as late as the 1880s.
timeline.quote: The release of the 1885 Sanborn fire insurance map supports that the building material of the Italianate style residence on the corner of Church and Cherry Streets was brick.

timeline.detail: A nine bay Italianate building was built on the northwest corner of Church and Cherry in 1899.
timeline.quote: The final structural modification to be made on this sector of Church Street was the construction of the nine bay Italianate style building on the northwest corner of Church and Cherry Streets in 1899.

timeline.detail: Woolworth's 5 and 10 Cent Store, managed by E. B. Wood, occupied the ground floor at 37-39 Church from 1899 until it closed in 1998.
timeline.quote: Since 1899 this was the site of F. W. Woolworth Company 5 and 10 Cent Store (Figure 3) managed by E. B. Wood.

timeline.detail: By 1944 Woolworth's had taken over the ground floor of the neighboring building.
timeline.quote: By 1944 with growing business, Woolworth’s expanded and took over the ground floor of the neighboring contemporary building.

timeline.what: Two buildings demolished; Art Deco store built
timeline.detail: Woolworth's demolished the two buildings and built a new Art Deco structure, one of its largest New England stores.
timeline.quote: In 1964 Woolworth’s opened one of its largest department stores in New England after it had demolished the two buildings and constructed a new Art Deco style structure

timeline.detail: A glass canopy was added to the front of the building in 1981.
timeline.quote: a glass canopy was added in 1981 to the front of the building

timeline.detail: Woolworth's closed in 1998 and the building then served chain stores including Old Navy.
timeline.quote: The Art Deco style structure has since served a variety of chain stores, including Old Navy after Woolworth’s closed in 1998.

timeline.what: Panera Bread and Outdoor Gear Exchange
timeline.detail: The building was later split between Panera Bread and Outdoor Gear Exchange; no years given.
timeline.quote: It was later split between Panera Bread and Outdoor Gear Exchange.

timeline.detail: After Panera closed, Outdoor Gear Exchange expanded through the entire building, which it occupied as of 2018.
timeline.quote: Outdoor Gear Exchange jumped at the opportunity to expand its business throughout the entire building.

photos.caption: 1945 view of F. W. Woolworth Company looking west
Post 1964 F. W. Woolworth building reconstruction looking northwest

timeline.what: Central House hotel, L. D. Turrill
timeline.detail: L. D. Turrill was proprietor of the Central House, advertised in the 1865 city directory.
timeline.quote: In 1865, L. D. Turrill was the proprietor of the Central House.

timeline.detail: Colvin kept an office in his private residence at 49 Church Street in 1881.
timeline.quote: H. E. Colvin, who was a homeopathic physician and surgeon, with an office he operated out of his private residence at 49 Church Street in 1881.

timeline.what: Central House demolished; Central House Block
timeline.detail: The 1885 Sanborn map shows the Central House demolished and replaced by a six bay Italianate building renamed the Central House Block.
timeline.quote: The 1885 map showed that the Central House had been demolished and was replaced by a six bay Italianate style building (Figure 2) renamed the Central House Block.

timeline.what: Central House Block demolished for Kresge
timeline.detail: The block was demolished for S. S. Kresge Company's new department store and renamed the Kresge Block.
timeline.quote: In 1930 the Central House Block was demolished to make room for S. S. Kresge Company’s new department store.

timeline.detail: Kresge operated about 35 years before going out of business in 1965.
timeline.quote: In 1965 when it went out of business it was replaced by the Jupiter department store.

timeline.detail: Jupiter replaced Kresge in 1965; its run ended when the Kresge Block was torn down in 1976.
timeline.quote: Jupiter’s time on Church Street was short lived when the Kresge Block was torn down for the construction of the new suburban styled mall in 1976.

timeline.detail: The mall, designed by Alexander & Truex Architects, was Burlington's primary bicentennial project and part of an urban renewal zone; its open metal entrance was later enclosed in brick.
timeline.quote: Nearly five decades ago the mall was constructed in the 1976 as part of an Urban Renewal zone in Burlington that leveled a 27-acre portion of the downtown.

timeline.what: Mall bought by Don Sinex for CityPlace
timeline.detail: Developer Don Sinex bought the mall for $25 million to build the 14 story, $225 million CityPlace Burlington.
timeline.quote: In 2013 the mall was purchased for $25 million by developer, Don Sinex to construct a new tall building (Figure 5) capped off at 14 stories called CityPlace Burlington.

timeline.detail: Delays in August 2018 slowed construction; Sinex hoped to open retail and parking by early 2020 and finish by January 2021. As of 2018, 49 Church Street is the entrance to what remains of the mall.
timeline.quote: Recent delays in August 2018 have delayed Sinex’s construction progress, but he hopes to have retail space and the parking garage open by early 2020

photos.caption: 1880s view of Church Street looking northwest
Proposed design for CityPlace Burlington redevelopment looking southwest
1946/1947 McAllister view of S. S. Kresge department store looking northwest
November 2018 view of the construction zone behind L. L. Bean, where the mall lobby used to be

timeline.detail: The 1894 Sanborn map shows the remaining lot space filled by the three bay masonry Barrows Block with elliptical windows and a spire. The page gives no street number.
timeline.quote: The 1894 Sanborn is notable because the remaining lot space had been filled by the construction of the Barrows Block.

timeline.detail: The three story Italianate Union Block first appears on the 1869 Sanborn map.
timeline.quote: In the 1869 Sanborn Fire Insurance Map the Union Block, 57-59 Church Street, and the Central Block, 61-75 Church Street (Figure 6) first appeared

timeline.what: Shedd and Walkers, glass and tinware
timeline.detail: J. A. Shedd is listed in the Union Block in partnership with Walkers, a glass and tinware dealer; no year in the text.
timeline.quote: Shedd is listed again in the Union Block in a business partnership with Walkers who was a dealer in glass and tinware.

timeline.detail: Dressmaker Bertha Church first appears living on the second floor of 59 Church Street.
timeline.quote: Bertha Church first appeared in 1940 when she lived on the second floor of 59 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Demolished in the 1970s during the urban renewal project that produced the mall; two small ground floor shopfronts replaced it.
timeline.quote: The fashionable, three story Union Block was demolished in the 1970s as part of the Urban Renewal project

timeline.detail: As of 2018, Hatley is at 59 Church Street and Zinnia's at 57.
timeline.quote: Hatley is located at 59 Church Street and Zinnia’s at 57 Church Street.

photos.caption: October 2018 view of Burlington Town Center Mall and shops along Church Street looking northwest

timeline.detail: Built in the 1860s; the page calls it the catalyst for commercializing this block.
timeline.quote: The construction of the Central Block in the 1860s created a catalyst

timeline.detail: The Italianate brick Central Block first appears on the 1869 Sanborn map.
timeline.quote: In the 1869 Sanborn Fire Insurance Map the Union Block, 57-59 Church Street, and the Central Block, 61-75 Church Street (Figure 6) first appeared

timeline.what: Ground floor shops, upper floor apartments
timeline.detail: Most businesses are confined to the ground floor with apartments and studios above.
timeline.quote: most businesses have been confined to the ground floor with apartments and studio spaces on the upper two stories.

timeline.detail: Bertha Church first appears in 1940, living at 59 Church Street and working as a dressmaker.
timeline.quote: Bertha Church first appeared in 1940 when she lived on the second floor of 59 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Mrs. Church added corsetiere services in 1960.
timeline.quote: Mrs. Church later added corsetiere services in 1960.

timeline.detail: The business moved across the street to 68 Church Street and later became Bertha Church, Inc. Intimate Apparel Shop.
timeline.quote: In 1963, Bertha Church moved across the street to 68 Church Street.

timeline.detail: In 1992 the shop was at 66 Church Street; it later moved across the street to 61. The page says it is owned by Tom Racine and managed by Jeanette Racine.
timeline.quote: In 1992, Bertha Church: Intimate Apparel, was located at 66 Church Street, but transitioned across the street to 61 Church Street.

timeline.what: Hatley: The Little Blue House founded
timeline.detail: The children's clothing store is a Hatley subsidiary; the company started up in 1986.
timeline.quote: Hatley: The Little Blue House as the company is known starts up in 1986.

timeline.detail: Opened at 65 Church Street in 1983.
timeline.quote: It is located at 65 Church Street and was opened in 1983.

timeline.detail: Incorporated in 1879 and located on the upper levels of the Central Block at 73 Church; moldings, picture frames, and photographic supplies.
timeline.quote: One such business was L. G. Burnham & Company, incorporated in 1879. L. G. Burnham & Company was located on the upper levels of the Central Block at 73 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Burnham's successor W. K. Menns expanded the offerings in 1884.
timeline.quote: L. G. Burnham’s successor, W. K. Menns was an artistic photographer who expanded the assortment of offers and services in 1884.

timeline.detail: By 1889 the art store expanded into 71 Church Street with a jewelers and opticians division.
timeline.quote: By 1889 L. G. Burnham & Company expanded its art store over into 71 Church Street and opened a jewelers and opticians division.

timeline.detail: Ken's first appeared in 1978 at 71-73 Church Street and is described as still a regular part of the street.
timeline.quote: Ken’s Deli and Pub first appeared on Church Street in 1978 (Figure 8) and occupied 71-73 Church Street.

photos.caption: 1978 view of the Central Block looking north towards the Unitarian Church

timeline.what: R. B. Stearns and Co., druggist
timeline.detail: Listed at 75 Church on the Bank Street corner in the 1900 directory; the page says the site hosted druggist and dentistry services for over 100 years.
timeline.quote: In the 1900 Burlington city directory, druggist R. B. Stearns and Co. was listed at 75 Church on the corner where it intersects Bank Street.

timeline.detail: Listed at 75 Church but operating from the Central Block's second floor.
timeline.quote: In 1941 the Beebe Pharmacy was listed at 75 Church, but was operating out of the second floor of the Central Block.

timeline.detail: One of the longest running pharmacies on Church Street, from 1943 into the 1990s; managed late in its run by Liza Pain.
timeline.quote: Out of all three pharmaceutical companies, the Kelley Pharmacy was established the longest between 1943 and the 1990s.

timeline.detail: The clothing and accessories boutique replaced Kelley Pharmacy and was still in business as of 2018.
timeline.quote: After Kelley Pharmacy went out of business it was replaced by Monelle Vermont, a clothing and accessories boutique which is still in business today.

pages.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018

places.address: East side of Church St between College and Bank (block overview)

photos.caption: 1860s photograph of the east side looking south from near Bank Street; shows Wingate Block (104) and Seymour's Building (102)
photos.credit: Burlington Photo Files, Street Views, Courtesy of University of Vermont Special Collections

photos.caption: 1862 Burlington Free Press map of the block's occupants
Map of addresses on the block
View from Auld's Picturesque Burlington showing the first Howard National Bank, Brodie Block cornice, and new Warner Block
photos.credit: Joseph Auld, Picturesque Burlington (Free Press Association, 1893), 244

photos.caption: Modern view of the block looking north from Church and College

timeline.detail: A three-and-a-half story Federal brick building seen in the early 1860s photo is potentially the L-shaped structure on Young's 1830 plan.
timeline.quote: This is potentially the large L-shaped structure which occupies the space in Ammi Burnham Young’s 1830 Plan of Burlington Village.

timeline.detail: A new three-and-a-half story brick bank building, likely Romanesque Revival, was built for the First National Bank.
timeline.quote: In 1867, a new three-and-a-half story brick building was built for the First National Bank in 1867.

timeline.detail: The 1867 building was taken down and replaced with a three-story granite faced building for the new Howard Bank.
timeline.quote: In 1902, this building was taken down, and replaced with yet another three-story, granite faced building for the new Howard Bank.

timeline.detail: The 1862 map caption says Herrick appears to have owned the 114 property until his estate sold it in 1905; he may have built a three-story structure there around 1867.
timeline.quote: Herrick appears to have owned the property up until 1905, when his estate sold it to the Chittenden County Trust Company.

timeline.detail: The three-story Italianate building at 114 housed Beeman's dry goods, cloaks, and suits store; the Fig. 18 postcard dates it to c. 1903 or 1904.
timeline.quote: B.B. Beeman & Co. continued the tradition of selling dry goods, cloaks, and suits from this location.

timeline.what: 114 sold for Chittenden County Trust Company
timeline.detail: The Herrick estate sold the store to create a new banking house for the Chittenden County Trust Company.
timeline.quote: Ultimately in 1905, the estate of S.L. Herrick sold the store with the intentions of creating a new banking house for the Chittenden County Trust Company.

timeline.detail: After Beeman's lease expired April 1, 1906, architect W.R. Wilcox gave the store a new front facade and interior.
timeline.quote: Upon the expiration lease on April 1st, 1906, Mr. Beeman’s store would be extensively renovated, with a new front façade and transformed interior.

timeline.detail: The bank doubled its width northward; the 114 building was bought, torn down, and rebuilt as part of the bank, by Thomas M. James Company of Boston.
timeline.quote: In 1942, Howard National Bank expanded to the north, doubling the width of the existing building.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 the salon occupies the first and second floors of the bank building and its expansion.
timeline.quote: Stephen & Burns, an Aveda salon, currently occupies the first and second floors of the Howard Bank Building and its subsequent expansion into the space next door.

photos.caption: South facade of the former Howard National Bank Building, seen from College Street
West facade of the former Howard National Bank Building, 116-114 Church Street
Circa 1900s postcard showing the new Howard Bank and B.B. Beeman & Co. at 114
photos.credit: "Church Street, Burlington, VT" Made in Germany for Swasey, Importers, Portland, ME

photos.caption: Remodeled facade of 114, then Chittenden County Trust Company, beside Howard National Bank
photos.credit: "Church Street, Burlington, VT" Valentine & Sons' Publishing Co., Courtesy of University of Vermont Special Collections

photos.caption: Postcard c. 1903 or 1904 from Church and College showing the new Howard Bank and B.B. Beeman & Co.
photos.credit: "Church St., Burlington, VT" Published by C. H. Bessey, Courtesy of University of Vermont Special Collections

timeline.detail: The 1860s photo shows a narrow two-story Italianate building, but the 1869 Sanborn map shows a three-story gable roofed structure.
timeline.quote: However, the 1869 Sanborn map shows a three-story structure here with a gable roof.

timeline.detail: The grocery operated here for forty-one years before the 1947 fire forced it to relocate to South Burlington.
timeline.quote: A. Verret and Sons’ Grocery, who had operated from this location for forty-one years, were forced to relocate to a newly reconstructed store in South Burlington.

timeline.detail: On June 19, 1947, a malfunctioning electric motor started a fire that destroyed the building.
timeline.quote: On June 19th, 1947, a malfunctioning electric motor started a fire, which destroyed the building.

timeline.detail: Wrecking crews razed the building on July 9, 1947, with tow-trucks pulling down the walls.
timeline.quote: On July 9th, 1947, wrecking crews razed the building, as tow-trucks pulled the walls down in a dramatic spectacle.

timeline.detail: A later two-story mid-century building stands on the site (no year given); as of 2018 Lippa Jewelers occupies it.
timeline.quote: A later “mid century,” two-story building was later constructed on the site, and still stands today. This space is currently occupied by Lippa Jewelers.

photos.caption: West facade of 112 Church Street, built after the Verret grocery was demolished

timeline.detail: The 1862 map caption says A.S. Dewey appears to have owned the two-story gable roofed building here until Kelsey and Brodie bought it.
timeline.quote: A.S. Dewey looks to have owned the two-story gable roofed building one door to the south, visible in Figure 1.

timeline.detail: A two-story Greek Revival building at 110 appears on the 1869 map as a dry goods store.
timeline.quote: The 1869 Fire Insurance Map of Burlington displays this building as a dry goods store.

timeline.detail: Kelsey and Brodie, partners in the boot and shoe business, erected the four-story brick Brodie Block in 1882.
timeline.quote: This block was erected in 1882 by Kelsey and Brodie, who were at the time in partnership in the boot in shoe business.

timeline.detail: A fire caused an estimated $60,000 loss, destroying half the third floor, all the fourth floor, and a third of the roof.
timeline.quote: damaged beyond repair in the June 3rd, 1894 fire, which had created an estimated loss of $60,000.

timeline.detail: After the 1894 fire D.A. Brodie bought out M.L. Kelsey and rebuilt; Pease and Manson clothing took the first floor, Miller & Miller veterinary surgeons the second. D.W.C. Clapp ran the rebuilding.
timeline.quote: Once complete, the first floor was occupied by the clothing store Pease and Manson.

timeline.detail: A fatal fire gutted the block, then owned by Mrs. Jeannine Hardy; a Winooski firm demolished it.
timeline.quote: In 1966, a fatal fire gutted the longstanding Brodie Block, which was owned by a Mrs. Jeannine Hardy.

timeline.detail: The lot stood vacant for four years.
timeline.quote: The lot stood vacant for four years until 1970, when local developer Antonio Pomerleau built the building which stands there now.

timeline.detail: Antonio Pomerleau built the current building, with shops below and offices and apartments above.
timeline.quote: The lot stood vacant for four years until 1970, when local developer Antonio Pomerleau built the building which stands there now.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 the two addresses hold these retail stores.
timeline.quote: These two addresses are currently occupied by the retail stores Tradewinds and Downtown Threads.

photos.caption: West facade of 110 and 108 Church Street, built 1970 by Antonio Pomerleau on the Brodie Block site

timeline.detail: A building with a similar footprint appears on Young's 1830 plan. The Fig. 8 caption says construction date is unknown but it likely dates to the early 1850s.
timeline.quote: In Ammi Burnham Young’s 1830 Plan of Burlington Village, a building with similar footprint can be seen.

timeline.detail: Importer and dealer in crockery, china, glassware, wallpaper, and cutlery.
timeline.quote: In 1858, the store was occupied by G.W. Baxter, an importer, jobber, and retail dealer in crockery, china, glassware, wallpaper, and table cutlery.

timeline.what: A. Prouty Jr., boots and shoes
timeline.detail: By 1859 the store was occupied by Prouty; the building was later sold to C.W. Wingate and Son of Boston (no year).
timeline.quote: By 1859, the store was newly occupied by A. Prouty Jr., a boot and shoe dealer.

timeline.what: Elevated wooden platform to Tin Shop
timeline.detail: Maps from 1869 through 1919 show an elevated wooden platform beside 104 leading to a Tin Shop behind.
timeline.quote: All maps beginning in 1869 throughout 1919 denote the structure as an elevated wooden platform, which led to a “Tin Shop” located behind 104.

timeline.what: New York China and Tea Co.
timeline.detail: By 1883 the tea company opened a branch in Wingate's Block.
timeline.quote: By 1883, the New York China and Tea Co. had opened a branch within Wingate’s Block.

timeline.detail: Before 1885 the building's address was 154 Church Street.
timeline.quote: Prior to 1885, the building’s address was 154 Church Street.

timeline.detail: The 1885 and 1889 Sanborn maps split the space among a tea and coffee store, a gun and locksmith, and the Commercial Union Telegraph Company; maps through 1919 show the telegraph office.
timeline.quote: Sanborn Maps through 1919 show the spaces continued to be used as the telegraph office.

timeline.detail: The entire front of the Wingate Block was torn out and replaced with plate glass windows.
timeline.quote: In 1888, the entire front of the then Wingate Block was torn out, and replaced with plate glass windows.

timeline.detail: The News and Citizen reported additional construction and repairs on the Wingate block.
timeline.quote: In 1923, Morrisville’s local newspaper, the News and Citizen , reported that additional construction and repairs commenced on the Wingate block.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 FatFace occupies the main building; a narrow addition presumably built after 1919 holds Cosmic Grind.
timeline.quote: The main building is currently occupied by the retail store FatFace.

photos.caption: West facade of 106 and 104 Church Street, the former Wingate Block, with the narrow Cosmic Grind addition

timeline.detail: The 1869 Sanborn map shows this three-story building at 152 Church Street as Seymour's Building, a dry goods store and warehouse.
timeline.quote: The Sanborn Fire Insurance Map from 1869 displays this three-story structure at 152 Church Street as Seymour’s Building.

timeline.what: Gable roof shown; false front later
timeline.detail: The 1877 bird's eye view still shows the gable roof, so the Italianate false front and cornice perhaps date to the 1880s.
timeline.quote: In the 1877 Birds Eye View of Burlington, the building is illustrated with its gable roof, perhaps dating the false front to the 1880s.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 the retail store Expressions occupies the space.
timeline.quote: This space is currently occupied by the retail store Expressions.

photos.caption: West facade of Seymour's Building, 102 Church Street, which retains its original gable roof behind a false front

timeline.detail: By 1885 Sanborn maps show a two story stone hardware store with brick veneer; earlier a small two-story Federal style brick building stood here.
timeline.quote: By 1885, the building is depicted in Sanborn Maps as a 2 story stone hardware store, with brick veneer around all exterior walls.

timeline.detail: The Vermont Division for Historic Preservation says the Isham Brothers built it in 1894 as an investment property.
timeline.quote: According to the Vermont Division for Historic Preservation, this building was built in 1894 by the Isham Brothers as an investment property.

timeline.detail: By 1923 Hagar Hardware moved here from 174 College Street and operated until 1978.
timeline.quote: Hagar Hardware continued to operate out of 98 Church Street up until 1978.

timeline.what: Jess Boutique and Bao Tak Fai Tai Chi Institute
timeline.detail: As of 2018 these two tenants occupy the space.
timeline.quote: The space is currently occupied by Jess Boutique, as well as Bao Tak Fai Tai Chi Institute.

photos.caption: West facade of the Isham Block, 100 and 98 Church Street, home of Hagar Hardware for over 56 years

timeline.detail: The 1869 Sanborn map shows two early two-story wood frame buildings, the larger a shoe factory.
timeline.quote: The larger of the two is recorded as a shoe factory.

timeline.detail: By 1885 three two-story wood framed buildings spanned the lot.
timeline.quote: By 1885, three, two-story wood framed buildings spanned the lot.

timeline.detail: Designed by W.H. Townsend and funded by Mrs. Wheeler, who inherited the lot and funds from her uncle Charles F. Warner; Guy N. Willard did the masonry and plastering.
timeline.quote: This block was built in 1886, funded by a Mrs. Wheeler, who inherited “the lot and ample funds for the erection of the block” from her uncle, Mr. Charles F. Warner.

timeline.what: Opens; Geo. H. Kinsley first tenant
timeline.detail: Ready for occupancy January 1, 1887; the lower store, then the deepest in the city, was first occupied by Geo. H. Kinsley.
timeline.quote: The building was ready for occupancy as of January 1st, 1887. The lower store (which was 22 by 135 feet at the time) was first occupied by Geo. H. Kinsley.

timeline.what: Stella Mae, Warner Supply, B. Good, Free People
timeline.detail: As of 2018: 96 has Stella Mae and Warner Supply, 94 is apartments and condos, 92 is B. Good, 90 is Free People.
timeline.quote: 96 Church Street is currently occupied by both Stella Mae and Warner Supply.

photos.caption: West facade of the Warner Block, 96 to 90 Church Street, designed by W.H. Townsend in 1886

timeline.detail: The 1885 Sanborn map shows a wood-framed structure, three stories in front and two in back.
timeline.quote: Just 4 years earlier, the Sanborn map depicted a wood-framed structure, three-stories tall in front, two in back.

timeline.detail: The lot was vacant on the 1889 Sanborn map; G.D. Weller, then city treasurer, began a new block in 1889, with masonry by Heman Crooker.
timeline.quote: According to a September 6th, 1889 Burlington Independent article, Mr. G.D. Weller (“though advanced in years”) began building a new business block.

timeline.detail: By 1890 the first story was occupied by Soule & Co.
timeline.quote: By 1890, the first story had been occupied by Soule & Co., a boot and shoe dealer.

timeline.detail: A basement fire nearly destroyed the building; the Burlington Military Band, rehearsing upstairs, raised the alarm.
timeline.quote: In 1932, the building was almost destroyed by a fire in the basement.

timeline.what: Asiana Noodle House and Saratoga Olive Oil
timeline.detail: As of 2018, 88 is Asiana Noodle House and 86 is the Saratoga Olive Oil Company.
timeline.quote: 88 Church Street is currently occupied by Asiana Noodle House. 86 houses the Saratoga Olive Oil Company.

photos.caption: West facade of the Weller Block, 88 and 86 Church Street, built 1889 by G.D. Weller

timeline.detail: The text says construction probably dates to the mid-1860s; the Fig. 13 caption says approximately the early 1860s.
timeline.quote: Based on its Italianate styling and similarity to its neighbor 80 Church Street, the construction for this building probably dates to the mid-1860s.

timeline.detail: The 1869 Sanborn map shows a three-story structure of similar footprint, without cornice.
timeline.quote: The 1869 Sanborn Map depicts a three-story structure of similar footprint, without cornice.

timeline.detail: By 1885 the building is shown as wood framed with a brick facade and wood cornice.
timeline.quote: By 1885, Sanborn Maps display the building as wood framed with a brick façade and wood cornice facing Church Street.

timeline.detail: By 1906 the building appears to be entirely brick.
timeline.quote: By 1906, it appears to have changed to entirely brick construction.

timeline.what: Home of Mr. and Mrs. G.F. Collison
timeline.detail: Owners of the millinery next door at 80; Mr. Collison may have run a machine shop on the first story. No year in text.
timeline.quote: 84 Church Street was home to Mr. and Mrs. G.F. Collison, owners of the millinery store one door to the north (80 Church Street).

timeline.detail: As of 2018 The Body Shop occupies the first floor, with apartments above.
timeline.quote: This first floor of this building is now occupied by The Body Shop, with apartments in the two stories above.

photos.caption: West facade of 84 Church Street, approximately early 1860s

timeline.what: Built for Fisher & Loomis Dry Goods
timeline.detail: Believed built in 1865; Fisher & Loomis opened here December 12, 1865.
timeline.quote: Fisher and Loomis opened their store here on December 12th, 1865.

timeline.detail: Between 1869 and 1871 Fisher & Loomis relocated from the corner of Church and Bank to 87 Church Street.
timeline.quote: Between 1869 and 1871, Fisher & Loomis relocated from the corner of Church and Bank to 87 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Mrs. Collison opened a model millinery and ladies store, run until the early 1890s.
timeline.quote: In 1887, Mrs. G.F. Collison (who owned the next-door building at 82 (now 84) Church Street opened up a “model millinery and ladies store” in the building.

timeline.detail: By 1906 the candy shop had opened; it operated over 50 years until closing in 1960.
timeline.quote: The candy shop operated for over 50 years, until it closed in 1960.

timeline.detail: By 1961 the building was vacant.
timeline.quote: By 1961, the building was vacant.

timeline.what: TD Bank and Marketplace Dental Associates
timeline.detail: As of 2018 TD Bank is at 80 and Marketplace Dental Associates above at 82; the third story is housing.
timeline.quote: Currently, 80 Church Street is occupied by TD Bank, and Marketplace Dental Associates occupies the floor above (82).

photos.caption: The Fisher Block, 82-80 Church Street, seen from Bank and Church

places.address: West side of Church St between King and Maple (block overview)

timeline.detail: An 1830 map shows the block used for a brickyard and a ravine containing railroad tracks; Church Street then ended at Pine Street, now King Street.
timeline.quote: This map shows that the west block of Church Street between King and Maple Street was used for a brickyard and a ravine.

timeline.detail: By 1853 Church Street extended two blocks south and the block was divided into parcels, with a structure at King and Church.
timeline.quote: By 1853, Church Street had extended two blocks south and the west block had been divided into parcels with a rectangular structure placed at the corner of King and Church.

timeline.detail: The ravine is absent on an 1869 map, though the 1877 bird's eye view shows a stone drainage culvert in the same spot.
timeline.quote: It is absent from the block in an 1869 map although, a stone drainage culvert can be seen in the same spot of the ravine in the 1877 Birds Eye View map

timeline.detail: A skating rink and annex at Church and King burned October 10, 1917, costing seventy jobs and $50,000 in damage; heat and water damaged every house on the block.
timeline.quote: A skating rink and annex building caught fire on the corner of Church Street and King Street on October 10, 1917.

photos.caption: Sketch map of Church Street between King Street and Maple Street, west block
Birds Eye View of Burlington and Winooski 1877
photos.credit: Courtesy UVM Special Collections, E. Meilbek

photos.caption: View of Church Street between Maple and King looking northwest, west block

timeline.detail: The name D. Blackman appears at the King and Church corner on an 1862 map. The page calls this the oldest structure on the block; build year unknown.
timeline.quote: the name, D. Blackman, was finally put on a map in 1862 in the same corner.

timeline.detail: The house first appears in directories in 1884, addressed to King Street; grocer A.L. Barrows lived there afterward.
timeline.quote: This house did not identify by an address in the city directories until 1884 and was listed as 139 King Street instead of Church Street.

timeline.detail: A produce dealer began living in the home sometime between 1890 and 1892.
timeline.quote: A.L Barrows, a very well-known grocer, began residing in this house until a produce dealer started residing in the home somewhere between 1890 and 1892.

timeline.detail: Hathorne partnered with Van A. Nye selling produce at the corner until moving to a store in 1893.
timeline.quote: This produce dealer, Henry G. Hathorne became business partners with Van A. Nye in 1892 and they started to sell produce together at the corner of King and Church until moving to a store in 1893.

timeline.detail: Hathorne took in teacher boarders in 1895, widening to other low-income workers in 1897.
timeline.quote: Hathorne began to open up his home for boarding in 1895 to teachers and it grew to individuals with other low-income professions in 1897.

timeline.detail: Lived in by a single family from 1903 until 1948.
timeline.quote: The house was lived in by a single family from 1903 until 1948 and then the dwelling became 199 Church Street in 1949.

timeline.detail: A hose was kept on the corner house for an hour during the 1917 fire.
timeline.quote: The house on the corner of King and Church was said to be in danger of the flames so a water hose was kept on the structure for an hour.

timeline.detail: The dwelling became 199 Church Street in 1949.
timeline.quote: The house was lived in by a single family from 1903 until 1948 and then the dwelling became 199 Church Street in 1949.

timeline.detail: The building became a house and business when Peggy Ryan made gowns there.
timeline.quote: The structure became both a house and a business in 1951 when Peggy Ryan started making gowns out of her home until 1960.

timeline.detail: Great Northern Woodworks took over in 1978; as of 2018 it is Great Northern Construction, still in the building. The page's 1970 sentence is garbled.
timeline.quote: Great Northern Woodworks took over the building in 1978 along with other tenants.

timeline.detail: Two apartment buildings grouped as one property with seventeen units; both first appear in directories in 1897.
timeline.quote: they both first appear in the city directories in 1897.

timeline.detail: 205 was listed as Mary Riley's boarding house.
timeline.quote: 205 is listed as Mary Riley’s boarding house from 1908 until 1920.

timeline.detail: LaFrance Bowling Alley owner moved in 1930 and died between 1944 and 1946, around when the McAllister photo was taken.
timeline.quote: LaFrance first moved into the building in 1930 and passed away between 1944 and 1946

photos.caption: Circa 1945 view of 205 & 209 Church Street, and recent view
photos.credit: Louis McAllister, Courtesy UVM Special Collections; Kristi Bodine, 2018

timeline.detail: The first tenant listed was widow Margaret Kennedy in 1897.
timeline.quote: The first tenant listed at this address was Margaret Kennedy, a widow, in 1897.

timeline.detail: The page says the two-family home was built in 1899, after its first listed tenant.
timeline.quote: 211 Church Street, is a two-family home, built in 1899

timeline.detail: Only one person was listed at a time until 1949.
timeline.quote: Only one person at a time was listed at this location until 1949 when there were two tenants, one being Lucius Jackson.

photos.caption: Street view looking southwest of Church Street between King and Maple; 211 Church Street far left

timeline.detail: The address first appears in 1895: Joseph Lefebvre, carriage trimmer, and George E. McCannon, carriage painter. The original building no longer exists.
timeline.quote: The first tenant listed is Joseph Lefebvre, a carriage trimmer, who used this address as his shop along with George E. McCannon, a carriage painter.

timeline.detail: An 1893 ad calls Parry's shop at Church and Maple the largest in Burlington; he is listed at 217 the year after 1895 and left in 1904.
timeline.quote: Parry left his shop on Church Street in 1904

timeline.detail: Cummings replaced McCannon in 1898 and was gone the following year.
timeline.quote: In 1898, Issac Cummings took George E. McCannon’s spot as carriage painter

timeline.detail: Collins had his shop on the site from 1902 to 1934; its roof caught fire in the 1917 blaze.
timeline.quote: John Collins, a blacksmith arrived in 1902 and had his shop on the site until 1934.

timeline.detail: Joseph and Sam Agel ran a livery.
timeline.quote: the Agel Bros., Joseph and Sam, turned the shop into a livery in 1906 but only stayed until 1907.

timeline.detail: Carriage blacksmiths and painters and a carriage trimmer; Tuttle gone by 1912, Thompson by 1913.
timeline.quote: In 1909, E.P. Tuttle & Sons, carriage blacksmith and painters, had their shop next to John Collins as well as H.F. Thompson, a carriage trimmer.

timeline.detail: Richards took over in 1913 until 1915; the 1917 fire account still calls him the vulcanizer at 217.
timeline.quote: Thompson had left the property and Charles A. Richards, a vulcanizer, had taken over until 1915.

timeline.detail: Carriage manufacturer and blacksmith.
timeline.quote: William A. Robarge, carriage manufacturer and blacksmith, arrived in 1914 and stayed until 1920.

timeline.detail: A mid-modern two-family home built in 1939 after the site was an auto shop and furniture storage; still standing as of 2018.
timeline.quote: The fifth structure on the west block is a mid-modern-style, two-family home built in 1939

photos.caption: 217 Church Street
Newspaper article advertising Parry's Carriage Shop

timeline.detail: John W. Johnson ran his granite works next to his house at 221, which no longer exists, until retiring in 1932.
timeline.quote: he ran his granite works business next door to his house, at 221 Church Street, which no longer exists.

timeline.detail: A three-family Queen Anne home built in 1900; stone cutter John W. Johnson was its first resident and lived there until 1943.
timeline.quote: This address, 223 Church Street, first appears in the city directories in 1900 and John W. Johnson was its first resident.

photos.caption: 1929 ravine construction view of 223 Church Street, and modern view
photos.credit: Louis McAliister, Courtesy UVM Special Collections; Kristi Bodine, 2018

timeline.detail: A modern commercial building built 1948, first in directories in 1949.
timeline.quote: is a modern commercial building that was built in 1948.

timeline.detail: Formerly a glass blowing studio; as of 2018 home of Soundtoys with the front vacant.
timeline.quote: This structure was home to a glass blowing studio and is now the home of Soundtoys although, the front of the building is vacant.

pages.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018

places.address: Corner of Church and Main Streets

timeline.detail: Early in the 19th century Seth Pomeroy built a small cottage facing Main Street here.
timeline.quote: Early in the nineteenth century, Seth Pomeroy built a house at the corner of Church and Main Streets.

timeline.detail: By the 1830s John Johnson surveyed the expanded house and outbuildings, valued at $3,220.
timeline.quote: Overall, the house, outbuildings, and their contents were valued at $3,220.

timeline.detail: In the early 1850s Pomeroy sold the lot for $7,750 for a post office and custom house designed by Ammi Young.
timeline.quote: In the early 1850s, Pomeroy sold the house and lot to the United States Treasury for $7,750 to build a post office and custom house.

timeline.detail: The two-story main building was completed in 1857, though figure captions call it the 1855 Post Office.
timeline.quote: The main building of two stories was completed in 1857, with the third floor and mansard roof added in 1869-70

timeline.detail: A third floor and mansard roof were added in 1869-70.
timeline.quote: The main building of two stories was completed in 1857, with the third floor and mansard roof added in 1869-70

timeline.detail: The old building served until the early 1900s, when the Beaux-Arts Classical building still on the corner replaced it.
timeline.quote: This building served until the early 1900s, when it was replaced with the Beaux-Arts Classical Style building still standing on the corner of Church Street and Main

timeline.detail: Voters approved a bond to renovate the former post office, then an army reserve center, and the courts moved in.
timeline.quote: In 1974, Chittenden County voters approved a bond issue to renovate the former post office and custom house next door

photos.caption: Detail of John Johnson's survey of John Norton Pomeroy's house
Main Street front of the 1855 Post Office and Custom House, circa 1901
Interior view of a post office
1930s postcard of the post office from Main and Church, with the 1872 Courthouse

places.address: L-shaped brick dwelling south of the Custom House

timeline.detail: Maps from 1830 to 1869 show it; in 1862 it was the home of the custom house porter. Removed for the 1872 courthouse.
timeline.quote: In 1862, it was identified as the home of the "porter for Custom House," but the building was removed in conjunction with the building of the new Chittenden County Courthouse in 1872.

places.address: Chittenden County Courthouse (southern part of the Custom House lot)

timeline.detail: Second Empire courthouse by E. C. Ryer in redstone quartzite with Isle La Motte stone trim.
timeline.quote: In 1872, the fourth courthouse ( Figure 6 ) was built on the southern part of the Custom House lot, just fifty feet from the post office.

timeline.detail: Severely damaged by fire while still in use; woodwork salvaged, then demolished. The site is now a parking lot.
timeline.quote: the old courthouse was still in use when it was severely damaged by fire in 1982.

photos.caption: The 1872 Courthouse and 1855 Customs House, 1900-1905
Detail from Meilbeck's 1877 Bird's Eye View, looking east

timeline.detail: Built on filled ravine land as the temporary post office.
timeline.quote: It served as post office from 1906 to 1908, and then as a laboratory for the Vermont Department of Health.

timeline.detail: The lab moved to Colchester Avenue in 1919.
timeline.quote: Since 1919, when the laboratory moved to Colchester Avenue, it has been an apartment building.

timeline.detail: Apartments since 1919.
timeline.quote: Since 1919, when the laboratory moved to Colchester Avenue, it has been an apartment building.

timeline.detail: Built in the late 1890s on filled ravine land, with three floors and two turrets; apartments ever since.
timeline.quote: 190 Church Street was built in the late 1890s as apartments, and has been so ever since.

timeline.detail: A March 1961 fire injured two firemen and left more than thirty people homeless; rebuilt without the third floor or turret tops.
timeline.quote: In March 1961, a fire attributed to "children playing with matches" gutted the building.

timeline.what: Built for New England Tel. & Tel.
timeline.detail: Built as administrative offices for the telephone company.
timeline.quote: The building that now houses Burlington Telecom was built in 1951 as administrative offices for New England Telegraph & Telephone.

timeline.detail: UVM purchased the building in 1953; after the phone company left in the early 1970s it used it for library storage.
timeline.quote: the University of Vermont (which had purchased the building in 1953) attempted without success to sell the building

timeline.detail: Sold in 1980 and used as offices since, with tenants including Howard Mental Health, General Electric, and Long Distance North. As of 2018: City HR, Community Justice Center, Burlington Telecom.
timeline.quote: In 1980, the building finally sold and some of the proceeds were used to build the Library Research Annex on East Avenue.

photos.caption: Looking north along Church Street from the bottom of the old ravine; 200 Church Street at top

places.address: Ravine and parking lot (east side, Main to Maple)

timeline.detail: Tracks were built through the ravine in 1850.
timeline.quote: Vermont Central Rail Road built tracks there in 1850

timeline.detail: Tracks mostly abandoned after fall 1862 and removed sometime after June 1863; the ravine then became a sewer.
timeline.quote: The tracks in the ravine were mostly abandoned after the fall of 1862, and the tracks removed sometime after June 1863.

timeline.detail: Horatio N. Coon's proposal to dam the open sewer for ice skating was killed by the Board of Aldermen, though he advertised a rink anyway.
timeline.quote: In 1878, Horatio N. Coon made a proposal to the City

timeline.detail: The Free Press reported in December 1885 that the hollow had been raised to a gradual slope.
timeline.quote: "The immense hollow which formerly existed on Church street where it crosses the ravine," reported the Burlington Weekly Free Press in December of 1885

timeline.detail: McAllister photographed sewer repairs after a 1929 rain storm.
timeline.quote: Figure 9 shows repairs being made to the sewer following a 1929 "exceptional rain storm".

photos.caption: Detail from Presdee & Edwards' 1853 Map of Burlington showing the railroad through the ravine
McAllister photograph of sewer repairs in the ravine, with 174-176 Maple Street at left

places.address: Green Mountain Skating Rink site (in the ravine behind the post office)
aka: National Paper Tube and Box Company

timeline.detail: John R. McLaren's rink had about 20,000 square feet of rink space; roller skating in summer.
timeline.quote: In 1894, John R. McLaren opened a longer-lived (and apparently sewage-free) skating rink in the same place.

timeline.detail: Billed as the largest store in Vermont, with 35,000 feet of floor space; most of the building was converted to light industry in 1911.
timeline.quote: When the Green Mountain Skating Rink closed in 1902, the enormous space was turned into Salls' Exchange

timeline.what: Toy factory; National Paper Tube and Box Co.
timeline.detail: Most of the building was converted to light industry, including a toy and novelty factory and the box company.
timeline.quote: In 1911, most of the building was converted to light industry.

timeline.detail: Barely a month after September 1917 expansion plans, a spectacular fire damaged the complex; the box company moved to the Arbuckle Building, the toy factory did not recover. Sheds stayed as storage until the 1960s.
timeline.quote: Barely a month later, however, a "spectacular" fire did $50,000 in damage to the old skating rink complex.

photos.caption: Sherman's Military Band, 1882, a frequent performer at the rink
Advertisement for Salls's Exchange, Burlington Clipper, September 6, 1902

timeline.detail: Probably built around 1890 as a tenement for an absentee landlord; previously numbered 222-228 Church Street.
timeline.quote: this building was probably built around 1890 "as an income producing tenement for an absentee builder-landlord."

timeline.detail: The six original apartments were divided in the 1940s.
timeline.quote: The original six large apartments were divided in the 1940s to make sixteen units

timeline.detail: A fire damaged the second floor and the building became a focus for rent activists.
timeline.quote: In 1979, a fire damaged the second floor beyond what the landlord could afford to repair

timeline.detail: The King Street Revitalization Corporation bought it with a federal grant.
timeline.quote: The King Street Revitalization Corporation purchased the building with the assistance of a federal grant in 1980 and converted it to subsidized housing.
